title: Field gaugings at 176 Victorian stream gauges show no measurement cause for the post-1997 runoff deficit or the pre-1957 runoff excess (WMIS gaugings, 1911-2026)
abstract: Question: after 1997, Victorian runoff fell about 20% below its earlier relation to rain, and runoff before 1957 was above it. Published daily flow comes from stage records and rating curves, not from direct measurement. Can rating drift or flood-rating extrapolation make these changes? Approach: we used all public gaugings (direct discharge measurements) and rating tables of the Victorian Water Measurement Information System (76,994 gaugings, 179 gauges, 1886-2026). We compared each gauging with the published daily flow of the same day at 176 CAMELS-AUS gauges, and we measured the flow volume above the largest discharge gauged to date. Results: the median published 1997-2019 departure from the 1975-1996 rain relation was -22.7% (95% CI -27.1 to -18.7%). At steady flow, the gauged/published ratio changed by +0.1% (CI -0.3 to +0.4%; 26,106 gaugings) and had no step at 1997. Weighted by flow volume, it changed by -1.3% (CI -2.2 to -0.2%), and by -8% in the top 1% of flows. A measurement cause would need about +25%. Only 0.04% (median) of 1997-2019 flow was above the gauged range. Before 1957, a median 14% of flow volume was above the gauged range. But at 8 long gauges the 1911-1956 excess (+8.1%, CI 0.1 to 20%) stayed +7.7% when daily flow in both eras was capped at the largest pre-1957 gauging. Conclusion: in Victoria the post-1997 deficit and the pre-1957 excess are in the measured flows, not in ratings or extrapolation. Limitations: Victoria only; the test cannot see a constant bias of the gauging method; high-flow gaugings are few; the early test has 8 gauges. A fixed-rating re-rating method failed because stage datums changed, and we do not use it.
